paragraphs.text: VII.A. Normal Takeoff & Climb
Introduction
How
Takeoff & Climb 										AI.VII.A.K2
Normal Takeoff:
Airplane is headed into the wind, or the wind is very light
Surface is firm & of sufficient length to gradually accelerate to normal lift-off/climb speed
No obstructions on the takeoff path
RM: Runway Selection            AI.VII.A.R1
Limitations
Chapter 2 of the POH – Review applicable limitations
Can include Max weights, CG limitations, Crosswind & Tailwind restrictions, Runway length/width limitations, and more
Wind: Reasons to take off into the wind
Even motionless, a headwind will provide some airspeed due to wind moving over the wings
Decreased wheel speed needed to achieve flying speed
Shorter ground roll, less runway
Reduces wear/stress on the gear
Increased climb performance
RM: Tailwind increases required ground roll (RM: Effects of Tailwind) 			AI.VII.A.R2c
POH: Reference any max takeoff tailwind limitation
Crosswind: Reference any crosswind limitations (POH)
Ensure proficiency & within personal minimums
Aircraft Performance
Atmospheric Pressure
Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded, affecting density
Air density affects performance - As density increases, performance increases & vice versa
What Changes Air Density (DA)? Barometric Pressure, Temperature, Altitude, and Humidity
Density varies directly with pressure - As pressure increases, density increases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with temperature - As temp increases, density decreases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with altitude - As altitude increases, density decreases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with humidity – As humidity increases, density decreases & vice versa
How it affects Performance
As the air becomes less dense, it reduces:
Power, since the engine takes in less air
Thrust, since the propeller is less efficient in thin air (less air is moved for every rotation)
Lift, because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils
Runway Characteristics 									AI.VII.A.R2e
Surface: More friction associated with softer surfaces – increases takeoff roll
Gradient: Upsloping runway increases takeoff roll – reference Chart Supplement for gradient
Condition: Dry, wet, snow, ice, etc. affects braking effectiveness
Available Distance: Runway length available for takeoff
Performance Charts
Take into account all of the above information, and more (weight, configuration, etc.)
Reference takeoff & climb performance charts (generally, takeoff distance & takeoff climb)
Verify required distance and climb abilities are compatible with the runway/environment
Pilot Capability
Set and strictly adhere to personal minimums (runway length/width, winds, weather, etc.)
Ensure proficiency and safety
Runway Selection
Combination of all the above factors
Generally, boils down to Limitations + Performance + Personal Minimums
Configuration 											AI.VII.A.K4
Reference the POH and Before Takeoff checklist
Best Angle versus Best Rate of Climb 							AI.VII.A.K3
Best Rate of Climb (VY)
The airspeed producing the most altitude gain in the least time (max feet per minute)
Airspeed where the most excess power is available over that required for level flight
Used in normal takeoff and climb procedures
Best Angle of Climb (VX)
The airspeed that will produce the most altitude gain in a given distance
Airspeed where the most excess thrust is available over that required for level flight
VX will result in a steeper climb path, but will take longer to reach altitude than a climb at VY
Therefore, VX is used in clearing obstacles after takeoff
Normal Climb (Cruise Climb)
Performed at an airspeed recommended by the airplane manufacturer
Usually faster than the best rate of climb, and provides better cooling, control, and visibility
Normal Takeoff 										AI.VII.A.K1
Takeoff Roll
Taxi onto the Runway
Complete the before takeoff checklist prior to taxiing onto the runway
Controlled Airport
Never taxi onto a runway without a specific clearance
Clear the area prior to crossing the hold short lines
Uncontrolled Airport
Announce intentions on the CTAF to alert other aircraft of your position and intentions
Use other radio calls to build a mental picture of the traffic in the area and how it may affect you
Check the runway & final approach are clear
Entering any runway, verify the runway assigned matches the runway you are on
Aligning the aircraft
Align with the intended takeoff direction, straighten the nosewheel
Centerline site picture
Note ground points aligned with the runway to help maintain runway centerline in the climb
Release the brakes and advance power
After releasing brakes, smoothly and continuously advance to takeoff power
Ensure both feet are on the rudder pedals, and not pressing on the brakes
Expect left yaw when power is added – maintain centerline with right rudder
Gaining Speed
Check the engine instruments for proper operation, and verify airspeed indicator operation
Announce “gauges green,” “airspeed alive”
If improper indications, abort the takeoff and stop straight ahead
Use rudder to keep the nose of the airplane tracking down the centerline of the runway
Visual picture - Centerline between outer leg and control stick
Don’t use the brakes to steer
As speed increases, flight controls become more effective
Progressively smaller rudder pressures are necessary to maintain direction
Lift-Off
Rotation (VR)
As the aircraft reaches VR, gently pull back on the controls to establish a climb at VY
Pitch varies with weight and density altitude
Wings are kept level with ailerons
Use rudder pressure to stay straight & coordinated
Visually
Maintain centerline, pitch, bank with outside references & quick glances to instruments
90% outside, 10% inside
Initial Climb
Pitch for VY (VY + takeoff power = max altitude in min time)
Provides the most altitude in the case of an emergency
Visually
Adjust pitch and bank with reference to the natural horizon, verify with instruments
Make slight adjustments in relation to the natural horizon
Glance at the instruments to verify the new attitude is correct, repeat
Maintain extended centerline to avoid drifting into obstructions / other aircraft
Identify two points inline and ahead of the runway to use as a tracking reference
Scan vigilantly
Climb Checklist
Perform the climb checklist when at a safe altitude and under control (500’ AGL, or as required)
The checklist can be delayed to continue flying the aircraft – always fly first
Common Errors 										AI.VII.A.K5
Failure to review AFM/POH and performance charts prior to takeoff
Failure to adequately clear the area prior to taxiing into position on the active runway
Abrupt use of the throttle
Failure to check engine instruments for signs of malfunction after applying takeoff power
Failure to anticipate left turning tendency & Overcorrecting for left turning tendency
Relying solely on the airspeed indicator rather than developing an understanding of visual references and tracking clues of airplane airspeed and controllability during acceleration and lift-off
Failure to attain proper lift-off attitude
Inadequate compensation for torque/P-factor during initial climb resulting in a sideslip
Over-control of elevators during initial climb-out and lack of elevator trimming
Limiting scan to areas directly ahead of the airplane, causing a wing to drop immediately after lift-off
Failure to attain/maintain best rate-of-climb airspeed (VY) or desired climb airspeed
Failure to employ principles of attitude flying during climb-out, resulting in “chasing” the airspeed
Crosswind Takeoff & Climb 							AI.VII.A.K1, AI.VII.A.R2a
Basics
Basic steps are the same as a normal takeoff
Differences ensure centerline is maintained and a smooth takeoff with wind pushing across the runway
Aileron is applied into the wind, and rudder is used to maintain the centerline (sideslip)
Aileron keeps the wings level during the takeoff roll
Rudder keeps the nose tracking down the centerline
Right rudder is used to counter left turning tendencies, but:
If there is a crosswind from the left, additional right rudder will be required
If there is a crosswind from the right, less right rudder will be required
Once established in the climb, transition from the sideslip to a crab
Improper corrections can result in skipping, sideways movement, and side stress on the landing gear
Takeoff Roll
Taxi onto the Runway
Complete the before takeoff checklist prior to taxiing onto the runway
Clear the runway & approach
Verify correct runway
Align with the runway and straighten the nosewheel
Hold FULL aileron INTO the wind as the roll is started
Downward force on the upwind wing prevents it from raising
Release the brakes
Same as a normal takeoff, but with full aileron into the wind
Smoothly and continuously advance the throttle to takeoff power
Apply rudder to counter left turning tendencies & weathervane
Gaining Speed
As forward speed increases, ailerons become more effective, and the crosswind becomes more of a relative headwind
Aileron pressure into the wind should gradually be reduced
Adjust rudder to continue straight down the centerline
Lift-Off
In a significant crosswind, stay on the ground slightly longer for a smooth/definite takeoff
Apply back pressure to establish the pitch attitude for VY
Maintain crosswind corrections during liftoff to prevent drifting/skipping
Downwind wing and mainwheel may rise first
This is preferred to side skipping
When the plane leaves the ground, maintain drift correction
Visual: Maintain centerline, pitch/bank (slip) with outside references
Instruments: Verify pitch attitude to maintain VY
Initial Climb
Maintain a sideslip until the climb is established, then crab into the wind
Sideslip creates excess drag and reduces performance
Turn the nose into the wind to offset the wind with the wings level
Turn coordinator should be centered for coordinated flight
Visually
Use an outside scan to maintain pitch and bank
Use two points ahead of, and in line with the runway to maintain extended runway centerline
90% outside, 10% inside
Continue the same as a normal climb
Climb Checklist
Climb to 500’ AGL, and perform the ‘Climb Check’
Checklist can be delayed to fly the plane, if things are busy fly first
Common Errors 										AI.VII.A.K5
Using less than full aileron pressure into the wind initially on the takeoff roll
Mechanical use of aileron control rather than judging the lateral position of the airplane on the runway with visual clues and applying sufficient aileron to keep airplane centered laterally
Side-skipping due to improper aileron application
Inadequate rudder control to keep the airplane parallel to the centerline and pointed straight ahead in alignment with visual references
Excessive aileron input in the latter stage of the roll resulting in a steep bank into the wind at lift-off
Inadequate drift correction after lift-off
RM: Hazards & Emergencies
Rejected Takeoff 										AI.VII.A.R3a
Circumstances such as engine malfunctions, inadequate acceleration, runways incursion, ATC conflict, or another emergency can result in a takeoff having to be rejected on the runway
Ensure sufficient runway to accelerate to VR and stop on the runway
Prior to takeoff, identify a point at which the plane should be airborne
If not airborne, take immediate action
Rejected Takeoff Procedures
Follow procedures specified in the POH
Generally, power idle, and apply maximum braking while maintaining directional control
If required to shut down the engine due to a fire, or any other reason
Mixture to idle cutoff and magnetos off
Engine Failure											AI.VII.A.R3b
Time is of the essence
Unless prepared, there is a strong chance the pilot makes a poor decision or no decision
“We don’t rise to the level of our expectations; we fall to the level of our training”
Practice, Plan, then Brief the plan
Procedures
Step one, Maintain aircraft control
During the takeoff roll
Reject the takeoff and stop straight ahead
Immediately following takeoff
If there is sufficient runway available straight ahead, land on the remaining runway
Ensure you know how much runway you need (descent + landing distance)
During the takeoff climb
Aircraft will have full power, a high pitch attitude and right rudder
When the engine fails, lower the nose (best glide) and release right rudder
Once in control, establish a glide toward a landing area & start emergency procedures
Time and altitude permitting, notify ATC, accomplish applicable checklists, attempt a restart
Wind Shear 											AI.VII.A.R2b
What is it?
A sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or direction over a very small area
While wind shear can occur at any altitude, low-level wind shear is especially hazardous
Why is it dangerous?
Violent updrafts and downdrafts (up to 6,000 fpm) / abrupt changes to horizontal movement
Rapid changes in performance (tailwind shears to headwind, or headwind to tailwind)
Microbursts
Most severe type of wind shear
Characteristics
1-2 miles across
Lifespan of 5-15 mins.
Strong downdrafts
Strong turbulence
Headwind gains/losses of 30-90 knots
Indications
Visual – Intense rain shaft at the surface, but virga at cloud base; ring of blowing dust
Alerting Systems
LLWAS-NE, TDWR, and ASR-9 WSP systems installed at major airports
Many airports, especially smaller airports, have no wind shear systems
Handling Wind Shear
If possible, avoid it
Never conduct traffic pattern operations near an active thunderstorm
LLWAS (Low Level Wind Shear Alerting System) can warn of windshear
PIREPS
Approach into Wind Shear
Follow the POH procedures. If none, general techniques include:
Higher power and faster approach speed (add ½ the gust factor to approach speed)
Stay as high as feasible until necessary to descend
Go around at the first sign of an unexpected pitch or airspeed change
It is important to get FULL power and get the plane climbing
If the aircraft is descending toward the ground, ensure max power, increase pitch attitude as far as possible without stalling the airplane
Intent is to keep flying as long as possible in hope of exiting the shear
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28) Ch. 22 pgs. 7-18 for more details
Wake Turbulence (AC 90-23)									AI.VII.A.R2d
What is it?
Difference between the high and low pressure below/above the wing causes the air to move outward, upward and around the wingtips, leading to counter rotating vortices
All aircraft generate wake turbulence during flight
The larger the aircraft, the stronger the vortices
Vortices are strongest when the pressure differential is greatest (heavy, clean, slow)
Why is it Dangerous?
Rolling moments can exceed control authority and/or damage the aircraft
Wake turbulence can be encountered in any phase of flight (usually strongest at departure)
Vortex Behavior
Vortices are generated when an aircraft leaves the ground until it touches down
Remain about a wingspan apart and drift with wind at altitudes > a wingspan above the ground
Sink at a rate of several hundred FPM, slowing descent and diminishing in strength over time
When close to the ground (100-200’), they tend to move laterally at 2-3 knots
A crosswind decreases lateral movement of upwind vortex, increases downwind vortex
Light quartering tailwind can result in vortices along final approach centerline
Avoidance Procedures - Departing after a large aircraft:
On the same Runway
Rotate prior to their rotation point and climb above their climb path until turning clear
Executing a Low Approach, Missed Approach, or Touch-and-Go
Wait at least 2 minutes prior to takeoff
Vortex hazard may exist along the runway/in the flight path, particularly in a quartering tailwind
Intersection Takeoffs on the same Runway
Note the larger aircraft’s rotation point and rotate prior to it
Be alert to adjacent large aircraft operations, particularly upwind of the runway
Avoid headings that cross below the larger aircraft’s path
Distractions, Task Prioritization, SA 								AI.VII.A.R6
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Sterile flight deck during taxi, takeoff, and climb as well as descent and landing
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational Awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, especially in the traffic pattern
Maintain SA
Know where you are, what’s coming next, and stay ahead of the airplane
Be aware of other traffic. Build a 3d picture based on what you see, and hear on the radio
If SA or orientation is lost, admit it, and fix it
Disorientation: Get the aircraft to a safe attitude, airspeed, and altitude
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention full more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
If tasks are piling up, “Attack the closest alligator” – Deal with the most pressing problem
Safety is the number one priority - Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Low Altitude Maneuvering 									AI.VII.A.R5
A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially if slow, can result in a stall/loss of control near the ground
Low Altitude Stall/Spin
A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
If you get any indication of a stall at low level, recover, and climb to a safe altitude
Spin
A spin is a result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Recover at the first sign of a stall
Maintain coordination
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Recovery (PARE)
Power - Idle
Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
Once the spin has stopped, neutralize the rudders and raise the nose - be careful not to stall
Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries, follow the POH procedures
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) - AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range
Recommendations:
Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC
Know and fly above minimum published safe altitudes
If IFR, fly published procedures
Verify proper altitude, especially at night or overwater, through use of a correctly set altimeter
Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances
Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation
Don't operate below minimum safe altitudes if uncertain of position or ATC clearance
Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts and all available information
Use appropriate checklists
Know your aircraft and its equipment
Collision Hazards 										AI.VII.A.R4
Collision Avoidance
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Movements shouldn’t exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Clearing Procedures
Before Takeoff: Scan the runway and final approach for other traffic
Climbing: Execute gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Pattern: Scan for other traffic, enter traffic pattern at pattern altitude
Uncontrolled Fields: Be conservative with spacing during takeoff and in the pattern
Clearly communicate intentions & location
Operation Lights On (voluntary FAA safety program )
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft:
Same Category: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final approach have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Be aware of terrain that could cause a hazard during the climb or descent into the airfield
Study charts and use maximum elevation figures (MEFs) and other data
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strikes
Many structures can significantly affect safety below 500’ AGL and particularly below 200’ AGL
Obstacles can be found in the NOTAMs, and the Terminal Procedures (IFR document)
< 200’ AGL are unmarked/lighted power lines, antenna towers, etc.
Antenna towers can reach over 1,000-2,000’ AGL and their guy wires can extend 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires: Wires and lines span runway departures and landmarks pilots frequently follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc. (may not be lit)
Airport Surface
Be alert for vehicles, persons, wildlife, or anything that could cause a hazard
Reject or delay takeoff, as required. Go around if landing
Scan vigilantly during taxi for aircraft and obstacles - If unsure of clearance, stop until you’re sure
Runway Incursion 										AI.VII.A.R7
Be aware of the airplane’s position and be aware of other aircraft and vehicle operations at the airport
Readback all runway crossing and/or hold short instructions
Review airport layouts & know airport signage
Review NOTAMs
Study & use proper phraseology
Check for traffic before crossing any runway hold line or entering any taxiway
Turn on lights and the rotating beacon or strobes when taxiing
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

Runway Selection

Configuration 											AI.VII.A.K4
Reference the POH and Before Takeoff checklist

Best Rate of Climb (VY)
The airspeed producing the most altitude gain in the least time (max feet per minute)
Airspeed where the most excess power is available over that required for level flight

Performed at an airspeed recommended by the airplane manufacturer
Usually faster than the best rate of climb, and provides better cooling, control, and visibility
Normal Takeoff 										AI.VII.A.K1
Takeoff Roll
Taxi onto the Runway
Complete the before takeoff checklist prior to taxiing onto the runway
Controlled Airport
Never taxi onto a runway without a specific clearance
Clear the area prior to crossing the hold short lines
Uncontrolled Airport
Announce intentions on the CTAF to alert other aircraft of your position and intentions
Use other radio calls to build a mental picture of the traffic in the area and how it may affect you
Check the runway & final approach are clear
Entering any runway, verify the runway assigned matches the runway you are on
Aligning the aircraft
Align with the intended takeoff direction, straighten the nosewheel
Centerline site picture
Note ground points aligned with the runway to help maintain runway centerline in the climb
Release the brakes and advance power
After releasing brakes, smoothly and continuously advance to takeoff power
Ensure both feet are on the rudder pedals, and not pressing on the brakes
Expect left yaw when power is added – maintain centerline with right rudder
Gaining Speed
Check the engine instruments for proper operation, and verify airspeed indicator operation
Announce “gauges green,” “airspeed alive”
If improper indications, abort the takeoff and stop straight ahead
Use rudder to keep the nose of the airplane tracking down the centerline of the runway
Visual picture - Centerline between outer leg and control stick
Don’t use the brakes to steer
As speed increases, flight controls become more effective
Progressively smaller rudder pressures are necessary to maintain direction
Lift-Off
Rotation (VR)
As the aircraft reaches VR, gently pull back on the controls to establish a climb at VY
Pitch varies with weight and density altitude
Wings are kept level with ailerons
Use rudder pressure to stay straight & coordinated
Visually
Maintain centerline, pitch, bank with outside references & quick glances to instruments
90% outside, 10% inside
Initial Climb
Pitch for VY (VY + takeoff power = max altitude in min time)
Provides the most altitude in the case of an emergency
Visually
Adjust pitch and bank with reference to the natural horizon, verify with instruments
Make slight adjustments in relation to the natural horizon
Glance at the instruments to verify the new attitude is correct, repeat
Maintain extended centerline to avoid drifting into obstructions / other aircraft
Identify two points inline and ahead of the runway to use as a tracking reference
Scan vigilantly
Climb Checklist
Perform the climb checklist when at a safe altitude and under control (500’ AGL, or as required)
The checklist can be delayed to continue flying the aircraft – always fly first
Common Errors 										AI.VII.A.K5
Failure to review AFM/POH and performance charts prior to takeoff
Failure to adequately clear the area prior to taxiing into position on the active runway
Abrupt use of the throttle
Failure to check engine instruments for signs of malfunction after applying takeoff power
Failure to anticipate left turning tendency & Overcorrecting for left turning tendency
Relying solely on the airspeed indicator rather than developing an understanding of visual references and tracking clues of airplane airspeed and controllability during acceleration and lift-off
Failure to attain proper lift-off attitude
Inadequate compensation for torque/P-factor during initial climb resulting in a sideslip
Over-control of elevators during initial climb-out and lack of elevator trimming
Limiting scan to areas directly ahead of the airplane, causing a wing to drop immediately after lift-off
Failure to attain/maintain best rate-of-climb airspeed (VY) or desired climb airspeed
Failure to employ principles of attitude flying during climb-out, resulting in “chasing” the airspeed
Crosswind Takeoff & Climb 							AI.VII.A.K1, AI.VII.A.R2a
Basics
Basic steps are the same as a normal takeoff
Differences ensure centerline is maintained and a smooth takeoff with wind pushing across the runway
Aileron is applied into the wind, and rudder is used to maintain the centerline (sideslip)
Aileron keeps the wings level during the takeoff roll
Rudder keeps the nose tracking down the centerline
Right rudder is used to counter left turning tendencies, but:
If there is a crosswind from the left, additional right rudder will be required
If there is a crosswind from the right, less right rudder will be required
Once established in the climb, transition from the sideslip to a crab
Improper corrections can result in skipping, sideways movement, and side stress on the landing gear
Takeoff Roll
Taxi onto the Runway
Complete the before takeoff checklist prior to taxiing onto the runway
Clear the runway & approach
Verify correct runway
Align with the runway and straighten the nosewheel
Hold FULL aileron INTO the wind as the roll is started
Downward force on the upwind wing prevents it from raising
Release the brakes
Same as a normal takeoff, but with full aileron into the wind
Smoothly and continuously advance the throttle to takeoff power
Apply rudder to counter left turning tendencies & weathervane
Gaining Speed
As forward speed increases, ailerons become more effective, and the crosswind becomes more of a relative headwind
Aileron pressure into the wind should gradually be reduced
Adjust rudder to continue straight down the centerline
Lift-Off
In a significant crosswind, stay on the ground slightly longer for a smooth/definite takeoff
Apply back pressure to establish the pitch attitude for VY
Maintain crosswind corrections during liftoff to prevent drifting/skipping
Downwind wing and mainwheel may rise first
This is preferred to side skipping
When the plane leaves the ground, maintain drift correction
Visual: Maintain centerline, pitch/bank (slip) with outside references
Instruments: Verify pitch attitude to maintain VY
Initial Climb
Maintain a sideslip until the climb is established, then crab into the wind
Sideslip creates excess drag and reduces performance
Turn the nose into the wind to offset the wind with the wings level
Turn coordinator should be centered for coordinated flight
Visually
Use an outside scan to maintain pitch and bank
Use two points ahead of, and in line with the runway to maintain extended runway centerline
90% outside, 10% inside
Continue the same as a normal climb
Climb Checklist
Climb to 500’ AGL, and perform the ‘Climb Check’
Checklist can be delayed to fly the plane, if things are busy fly first
Common Errors 										AI.VII.A.K5
Using less than full aileron pressure into the wind initially on the takeoff roll
Mechanical use of aileron control rather than judging the lateral position of the airplane on the runway with visual clues and applying sufficient aileron to keep airplane centered laterally
Side-skipping due to improper aileron application
Inadequate rudder control to keep the airplane parallel to the centerline and pointed straight ahead in alignment with visual references
Excessive aileron input in the latter stage of the roll resulting in a steep bank into the wind at lift-off
Inadequate drift correction after lift-off
RM: Hazards & Emergencies
Rejected Takeoff 										AI.VII.A.R3a
Circumstances such as engine malfunctions, inadequate acceleration, runways incursion, ATC conflict, or another emergency can result in a takeoff having to be rejected on the runway
Ensure sufficient runway to accelerate to VR and stop on the runway
Prior to takeoff, identify a point at which the plane should be airborne
If not airborne, take immediate action
Rejected Takeoff Procedures
Follow procedures specified in the POH
Generally, power idle, and apply maximum braking while maintaining directional control
If required to shut down the engine due to a fire, or any other reason
Mixture to idle cutoff and magnetos off
Engine Failure											AI.VII.A.R3b
Time is of the essence
Unless prepared, there is a strong chance the pilot makes a poor decision or no decision
“We don’t rise to the level of our expectations; we fall to the level of our training”
Practice, Plan, then Brief the plan
Procedures
Step one, Maintain aircraft control
During the takeoff roll
Reject the takeoff and stop straight ahead
Immediately following takeoff
If there is sufficient runway available straight ahead, land on the remaining runway
Ensure you know how much runway you need (descent + landing distance)
During the takeoff climb
Aircraft will have full power, a high pitch attitude and right rudder
When the engine fails, lower the nose (best glide) and release right rudder
Once in control, establish a glide toward a landing area & start emergency procedures
Time and altitude permitting, notify ATC, accomplish applicable checklists, attempt a restart
Wind Shear 											AI.VII.A.R2b
What is it?
A sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or direction over a very small area
While wind shear can occur at any altitude, low-level wind shear is especially hazardous
Why is it dangerous?
Violent updrafts and downdrafts (up to 6,000 fpm) / abrupt changes to horizontal movement
Rapid changes in performance (tailwind shears to headwind, or headwind to tailwind)
Microbursts
Most severe type of wind shear
Characteristics
1-2 miles across
Lifespan of 5-15 mins.
Strong downdrafts
Strong turbulence
Headwind gains/losses of 30-90 knots
Indications
Visual – Intense rain shaft at the surface, but virga at cloud base; ring of blowing dust
Alerting Systems
LLWAS-NE, TDWR, and ASR-9 WSP systems installed at major airports
Many airports, especially smaller airports, have no wind shear systems
Handling Wind Shear
If possible, avoid it
Never conduct traffic pattern operations near an active thunderstorm
LLWAS (Low Level Wind Shear Alerting System) can warn of windshear
PIREPS
Approach into Wind Shear
Follow the POH procedures. If none, general techniques include:
Higher power and faster approach speed (add ½ the gust factor to approach speed)
Stay as high as feasible until necessary to descend
Go around at the first sign of an unexpected pitch or airspeed change
It is important to get FULL power and get the plane climbing
If the aircraft is descending toward the ground, ensure max power, increase pitch attitude as far as possible without stalling the airplane
Intent is to keep flying as long as possible in hope of exiting the shear
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28) Ch. 22 pgs. 7-18 for more details
Wake Turbulence (AC 90-23)									AI.VII.A.R2d
What is it?
Difference between the high and low pressure below/above the wing causes the air to move outward, upward and around the wingtips, leading to counter rotating vortices
All aircraft generate wake turbulence during flight
The larger the aircraft, the stronger the vortices
Vortices are strongest when the pressure differential is greatest (heavy, clean, slow)
Why is it Dangerous?
Rolling moments can exceed control authority and/or damage the aircraft
Wake turbulence can be encountered in any phase of flight (usually strongest at departure)
Vortex Behavior
Vortices are generated when an aircraft leaves the ground until it touches down
Remain about a wingspan apart and drift with wind at altitudes > a wingspan above the ground
Sink at a rate of several hundred FPM, slowing descent and diminishing in strength over time
When close to the ground (100-200’), they tend to move laterally at 2-3 knots
A crosswind decreases lateral movement of upwind vortex, increases downwind vortex
Light quartering tailwind can result in vortices along final approach centerline
Avoidance Procedures - Departing after a large aircraft:
On the same Runway
Rotate prior to their rotation point and climb above their climb path until turning clear
Executing a Low Approach, Missed Approach, or Touch-and-Go
Wait at least 2 minutes prior to takeoff
Vortex hazard may exist along the runway/in the flight path, particularly in a quartering tailwind
Intersection Takeoffs on the same Runway
Note the larger aircraft’s rotation point and rotate prior to it
Be alert to adjacent large aircraft operations, particularly upwind of the runway
Avoid headings that cross below the larger aircraft’s path
Distractions, Task Prioritization, SA 								AI.VII.A.R6
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Sterile flight deck during taxi, takeoff, and climb as well as descent and landing
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational Awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, especially in the traffic pattern
Maintain SA
Know where you are, what’s coming next, and stay ahead of the airplane
Be aware of other traffic. Build a 3d picture based on what you see, and hear on the radio
If SA or orientation is lost, admit it, and fix it
Disorientation: Get the aircraft to a safe attitude, airspeed, and altitude
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention full more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
If tasks are piling up, “Attack the closest alligator” – Deal with the most pressing problem
Safety is the number one priority - Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Low Altitude Maneuvering 									AI.VII.A.R5
A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially if slow, can result in a stall/loss of control near the ground
Low Altitude Stall/Spin
A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
If you get any indication of a stall at low level, recover, and climb to a safe altitude
Spin
A spin is a result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Recover at the first sign of a stall
Maintain coordination
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Recovery (PARE)
Power - Idle
Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
Once the spin has stopped, neutralize the rudders and raise the nose - be careful not to stall
Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries, follow the POH procedures
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) - AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range
Recommendations:
Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC
Know and fly above minimum published safe altitudes
If IFR, fly published procedures
Verify proper altitude, especially at night or overwater, through use of a correctly set altimeter
Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances
Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation
Don't operate below minimum safe altitudes if uncertain of position or ATC clearance
Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts and all available information
Use appropriate checklists
Know your aircraft and its equipment
Collision Hazards 										AI.VII.A.R4
Collision Avoidance
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Movements shouldn’t exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Clearing Procedures
Before Takeoff: Scan the runway and final approach for other traffic
Climbing: Execute gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Pattern: Scan for other traffic, enter traffic pattern at pattern altitude
Uncontrolled Fields: Be conservative with spacing during takeoff and in the pattern
Clearly communicate intentions & location
Operation Lights On (voluntary FAA safety program )
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft:
Same Category: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final approach have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Be aware of terrain that could cause a hazard during the climb or descent into the airfield
Study charts and use maximum elevation figures (MEFs) and other data
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strikes
Many structures can significantly affect safety below 500’ AGL and particularly below 200’ AGL
Obstacles can be found in the NOTAMs, and the Terminal Procedures (IFR document)
< 200’ AGL are unmarked/lighted power lines, antenna towers, etc.
Antenna towers can reach over 1,000-2,000’ AGL and their guy wires can extend 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires: Wires and lines span runway departures and landmarks pilots frequently follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc. (may not be lit)
Airport Surface
Be alert for vehicles, persons, wildlife, or anything that could cause a hazard
Reject or delay takeoff, as required. Go around if landing
Scan vigilantly during taxi for aircraft and obstacles - If unsure of clearance, stop until you’re sure
Runway Incursion 										AI.VII.A.R7
Be aware of the airplane’s position and be aware of other aircraft and vehicle operations at the airport
Readback all runway crossing and/or hold short instructions
Review airport layouts & know airport signage
Review NOTAMs
Study & use proper phraseology
Check for traffic before crossing any runway hold line or entering any taxiway
Turn on lights and the rotating beacon or strobes when taxiing
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: VII.B. Normal Approach & Landing
Introduction
How
RM: Runway Selection 								AI.VII.B.K3, AI.VII.B.R1
Limitations
Chapter 2 of the POH – Review applicable limitations
Can include Max weights, CG limitations, Crosswind/Tailwind restrictions, Runway length/width limitations, flap & gear extension speeds, stalls speeds, and more
Wind
Headwind decreases groundspeed and therefore landing distance
RM: Tailwind increases groundspeed and therefore landing distance 			AI.VII.B.R2c
Reference the POH for any max tailwind landing limitations
Crosswind: Reference any crosswind limitations (POH)
Ensure proficiency & within personal minimums
Aircraft Performance
Atmospheric Pressure
Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded, affecting density
Air density affects performance - As density increases, performance increases & vice versa
What Changes Air Density (DA)? Barometric Pressure, Temperature, Altitude, and Humidity
Density varies directly with pressure - As pressure increases, density increases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with temperature – As temp increases, density decreases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with altitude - As altitude increases, density decreases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with humidity – As humidity increases, density decreases and vice versa
How it Affects Performance
As the air becomes less dense, it reduces:
Power, since the engine takes in less air
Thrust, since the propeller is less efficient in thin air (less air is being moved for every rotation)
Lift, because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils
Density Altitude & Landing
Affects climb capability in the case of a go-around
Higher density altitude = higher true airspeed which increases the landing roll
RM: Runway Characteristics 									AI.VII.B.R2e
Surface: More friction associated with softer surfaces – decreases landing roll
Gradient: Down sloping runway increases landing roll – reference the Chart Supplement for gradient
Condition: Dry, wet, snow, ice, etc. affects braking effectiveness
Available Distance: Runway length available for landing
Performance Charts
Take into account all of the above information, and more (weight, configuration, etc.)
Reference landing & climb performance charts (generally, landing distance/performance & climb performance or balked landing climb charts)
Verify required distance and climb abilities are compatible with the runway/environment
Pilot Capability
Set and strictly adhere to personal minimums (runway length/width, winds, weather, etc.)
Ensure proficiency and safety
Runway Selection
Combination of all the above factors
Generally, boils down to Limitations + Performance + Personal Minimums
Downwind Leg
Parallel to the runway of intended landing, and normally at 1,000’ AGL (pattern altitude can vary)
Checklists
Before Landing Checklist at the midpoint of the downwind leg
Abeam the landing threshold
Begin descent
Reduce power, extend flaps as appropriate, and establish the initial descent airspeed
Maintain pattern altitude as the airplane slows to the descent speed
Begin the turn to base when at a 45o angle from the runway threshold
Shallow to medium bank – recall Rectangular Course procedures to compensate for wind
At the 45o point the airplane has descended approximately 200’ (800’ AGL) (varies with aircraft)
Base Leg
Leg prior to turning final; perpendicular to approach end of the runway
Position of the Base leg is one of the more important judgements made in any approach
Must judge the altitude / distance from which a stable descent results in landing at the desired spot
The distance of the base leg from the runway depends on altitude, wind, and the flaps used
Closer base leg if at a low altitude, flaps are used for a steeper descent, or a strong wind on final
Configuration
Establish the desired airspeed and configuration
Drift Correction – Maintain a ground track perpendicular to the runway
Common for a crosswind to push the airplane away from the runway
Crab into the wind to maintain the course
The Turn to Final
Medium to shallow bank turn should align the airplane with the centerline of the runway
No more than 30o of bank
Stall speed increases rapidly above 30o of bank
In the case a steep bank is necessary, a go-around is recommended
A descent of about 200’ is also made on the base leg (600’ AGL to start turn to final)
Varies based on aircraft, and conditions (terrain, obstructions, flaps, etc.). Adjust as required
On a 3o glidepath (which is equal to 300’ per nm), 600’ AGL is a two-mile descent to the runway
Final Approach
Longitudinal axis of is aligned with the center line and the final descent to the runway is made
Configuration – Generally, landing flaps and POH approach speed
Accomplish the Landing Checklist
Strong/Gusty Winds: Increase speed on final approach: Approach speed + ½ the gust factor
Use flaps as recommended in the POH
Landing Checklist
Stable Approach 										AI.VII.B.K2
Energy Management
Reference Appendix A. Energy Management for more detailed energy management concepts
Corresponding slides can be found in the slide’s appendix
Stable Approach: A constant glidepath towards a selected point on the landing runway
A stable approach is a safe approach
Unstable increases the risk of excessive rates of descent or slow airspeed close to the ground
Controlling the Descent: Power and pitch are adjusted to maintain a stable approach
The aircraft is below LDMAX and in the Region of Reverse Command
Pitch is used to maintain airspeed (too fast, pitch up; too slow, pitch down)
Power is used to maintain altitude / glidepath (too low, add power; too high, reduce power)
A change in either variable (pitch or power) requires a coordinated change in the other
If the approach is too high, reduce power and lower the nose to maintain airspeed
If the approach is too low, add power and raise the nose to maintain airspeed
Pitch for Airspeed, Power for Altitude
Angle of Descent
Aim Point
The point the plane would strike the ground if a constant glidepath was maintained (no flare)
The aim point should remain stationary in the windscreen
Aim point is not the spot the airplane will touchdown due to flare / float
Select an aiming point in front of the desired touchdown point (distance varies with aircraft)
Keep the aim point steady on the windscreen
If the point moves up on the windscreen, the airplane is getting too low
Add power and raise the nose to maintain airspeed
If the point moves down on the windscreen, the airplane is getting too high
Reduce power and lower the nose to maintain airspeed
Small, proactive corrections will result in a steady, stable approach to the aim point
Runway Image
A normal glidepath is 3o (300’ per nm descent)
Too High – The runway will elongate and become narrower (overhead view of the runway)
Too Low – The runway will shorten and become wider (flat view of the runway)
On Path – Runway shape (between high and low) remains the same but grows
The runway should maintain the same shape as the pilot continues down the approach path
Runway appears as a trapezoid – In the descent, it should maintain shape and grow
Visual Approach Lighting
Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI)
Visual descent guidance during approach
Visible from 3-5 miles during day and to 20 or more at night
Obstruction clearance within ± 10o of the centerline and 4 NM from the threshold
Two Bar VASI
Below glidepath: All red
On glidepath: Red over white (normally 3o)
Above glidepath: All white
Precision Approach Path Indicator (PAPI)
4 lights perpendicular to the runway
Provides visual descent guidance during the approach to a runway
On glidepath: 2 red & 2 white
Below glidepath: 3 or 4 red
Above glidepath: 3 or 4 white
Designed to reduce controlled flight into terrain and runway over/underruns
Effects of Wind
The greater the headwind, the lower the rate of descent
More time to cover the same distance
A lower headwind/greater tailwind = a higher the descent rate (less time)
The concepts discussed/site pictures remain the same - Still on a 3o glidepath
Landing Clearance
Ensure the controller gave you landing clearance, it was understood, and was read back
Roundout
Smooth transition from a normal approach attitude to a landing attitude, gradually rounding out the flight path to one that is parallel with, and within a very few inches of the runway
Estimating Height and Movement
Divide attention between a point just over the nose to the desired touchdown zone and back again
Visual focus should not be fixed on any one side or to any one spot ahead
Speed & Vision
Speed blurs objects at close range
The distance at which vision is focused should be proportionate to the speed of the airplane
As speed is reduced, the distance that the pilot focuses should be brought closer
Focusing too close will result in a blurred reference
Reactions will be too abrupt or too late (overcontrolling, high roundout/stalled landing)
When focused too far, the ability to judge the closeness of the ground is lost
Slow reactions (late or little to no flare, nose first landings)
If focus is gradually brought closer as speed is reduced the landing process is smoothed out
Starting the Roundout
Started approximately 10’ to 20’ above the ground (varies between aircraft and rate of descent)
Power is reduced to idle and back elevator is applied to gradually increase pitch attitude
Angle of attack is increased to allow the plane to settle slowly as airspeed decreases
Decreasing Lift, Increasing Pitch Attitude
With the power at idle, airspeed is decreasing – As airspeed decreases, the pilot increases the angle of attack which momentarily increases lift and decreases the rate of descent
Airspeed will continue to decrease causing lift to continue to decrease
This must be controlled by raising the nose and further increasing the AOA
Airspeed is being decreased to touchdown speed, while lift is being controlled with back pressure so that the airplane will settle gently onto the runway
Rate of the Roundout – Varies with the height above the ground, the rate of descent, and the pitch attitude
High Roundout: Executed slower to allow the plane to descend
Low Roundout: Execute faster to obtain the landing attitude before striking the runway
High Rate of Descent: Similar to low roundout, pitch attitude must be changed at a higher rate
Low Rate of Descent: Similar to high roundout, slow change in pitch is required
High Pitch Attitude (ex: full flap landing): Execute more slowly to prevent excessively high pitch
Low Pitch Attitude (ex: no flap): Execute faster to obtain attitude before striking runway
Note: Once the roundout has started, the elevator control should not be pushed forward
If necessary, relax back pressure or just hold it constant as airspeed decreases
Always keep one hand on the throttle (within reason)
Be prepared to apply immediate power or initiate a go around
Touchdown
The gentle settling of the airplane onto the landing surface at the minimum controllable airspeed with the airplane’s longitudinal axis parallel to its direction along the runway
Ideal Landing
Hold the airplane’s wheels a few inches off the ground as long as possible with the elevators
Increase back pressure to gently allow the main wheels to touchdown, followed by the nose
Longitudinal Axis
The longitudinal axis should be parallel to the direction the airplane is moving along the runway
Failure to do this can impose severe side loads on the landing gear
Rudder Control
Very little rudder is needed (no left turning tendencies with the engine at idle)
During landing, rudder is primarily used in crosswinds (more below)
After Touchdown
Maintain back-elevator pressure
Hold the nosewheel off the ground as the plane decelerates (assists with aerodynamic braking)
As speed decreases relax elevator pressure to allow the nosewheel to gently settle onto the runway
After-Landing Roll
Deceleration to the normal taxi speed, or when brought to a complete stop clear of the landing area
Directional Control on the Ground
Rudder
With the nosewheel on the ground, use the rudder to steer the airplane on the ground
Rudder effectiveness is dependent on airflow which is dependent on the speed of the plane
Aileron Control
Used to counter crosswinds and keep the wings level
As speed decreases the ailerons become less effective, and increasing aileron must be applied into a crosswind to keep the wing from rising
Be Alert
Remain vigilant throughout the landing roll and keep positive control of the airplane
Don’t assume that because the airplane is on the ground your work is done
Loss of Directional Control
May lead to an aggravated, uncontrolled, tight turn on the ground (ground loop)
Could impose a sideward force that could collapse the landing gear
Braking - Slows  the airplane, can also be used to aid in directional control when rudder is insufficient
Using the Brakes
Toe brakes – Slide feet up from the rudder pedals to the brake pedals (maintain rudder pressure)
Brake pressure is applied by pushing forward on the toe pedals
To turn with the brakes, apply pressure on one brake or uneven pressure on each brake
Effective Braking
Put maximum weight on the main wheels after touchdown
Nosewheel should be lowered to the runway to maintain directional control
After the nose is down, apply back pressure without lifting the nosewheel off the ground
Firmly, smoothly, and evenly apply the brakes
Max effectiveness is just short of the point where skidding occurs
If the brakes are applied so hard that skidding takes place, braking becomes less effective
Effectiveness is not enhanced by pumping (applying, releasing, and reapplying brake pressure)
Avoid a runway incursion
Have a plan to exit the runway (intended exit and stop point)
After Landing Checklist - Once safely clear of the runway
Common Errors (Normal Approach & Landing) 						AI.VII.B.K5
Failure to complete the landing checklist in a timely manner
Inadequate wind drift correction on the base leg
An overshooting, undershooting, too steep, or too shallow a turn onto final approach
A skidding turn from base to final as a result of overshooting/inadequate wind drift correction
Poor coordination during turn from base to final approach
Unstable approach
Failure to adequately compensate for flap extension
Poor trim technique on final approach
Attempting to maintain altitude or reach the runway using elevator alone
Focusing too close to the airplane resulting in a too high round out
Focusing too far from the airplane resulting in a too low round out
Touching down prior to attaining proper landing attitude
Failure to hold sufficient back-elevator pressure after touchdown
Excessive braking after touchdown
Loss of aircraft control during touchdown and rollout
RM: Crosswind Approach (RM: Effects of crosswind) 		AI.VII.B.K1, AI.VII.B.K4, AI.VII.B.R2a
Landing in which the wind is blowing across, rather than parallel to the landing direction. The same basic principles apply to a crosswind approach and landing as a normal approach and landing
Two Crosswind Methods
Crab Method – Not recommended
Easier to maintain during final approach, but requires a high degree of judgment and timing in removing the crab right before touchdown
How it Works
A crab is established into the wind so that the plane’s ground track remains aligned with the centerline
Crab is maintained until just prior to touchdown, when the longitudinal axis of plane is aligned with the runway to avoid touching down sideways
Sideslip (wing-low) Method – Recommended
Final Approach
Sideslip (Wing-Low)
Aileron for drift & Rudder for heading
Align the airplane’s heading with the centerline of the runway, noting the rate and direction of drift
Promptly apply drift correction by lowering the upwind wing
With wing lowered, the plane turns that direction
To compensate for the turn, use opposite rudder to align the longitudinal axis with the runway
Sideslipping so the flight path & ground track are aligned with the runway
Strong Crosswind
At some point there will be insufficient rudder to overcome the turn due to the steepened bank
If full rudder cannot prevent a turn, the wind is too strong (crosswind limit)
Find another runway
Stabilized Approach
Same as a normal approach, except with the added sideslip
Drag is increased and more power is necessary to maintain descent rate
Pitch for airspeed; Power for altitude
Roundout
Like a normal landing approach, but the crosswind correction is maintained to prevent drifting
Don’t level the wings – Keep the upwind wing down throughout the roundout
Leveling the wings will result in drifting, which will side loading the gear
Gradually increase the aileron and rudder pressure as the airplane slows
Touchdown
Touchdown on the upwind main wheel first
Maintain the crosswind corrections to prevent drift
During gusty or high wind conditions, prompt adjustments must be made
As momentum decreases, the downwind main wheel will settle onto the runway, then the nosewheel
Nose-wheel steering: Nosewheel will not be aligned with the runway due to rudder input
Relax rudder pressure as the nose touches down
After Landing Roll
Continue to maintain directional control with rudders and crosswind control with ailerons
Increase aileron as the airplane decelerates – full aileron into the wind when coming to a stop
Common Errors 										AI.VII.B.K5
Attempted landing in crosswinds that exceed the maximum demonstrated crosswind component
Undershooting or overshooting the turn from base leg to final approach
Inadequate compensation for wind drift on final approach
Unstable approach
Excessive sink rate or too low an airspeed from increased drag and reduced vertical lift during sideslip
Failure to touch down with the longitudinal axis aligned with the runway
Touching down while drifting
Excessive airspeed on touchdown
Failure to apply appropriate flight control inputs during rollout
Failure to maintain direction control on rollout
Excessive braking
Loss of aircraft control
RM: Hazards & Emergencies
Rejected Landing & Go-Around 								AI.VII.B.R3a
When to Go-Around
When it’s hazardous to continue or if you’re ever in doubt of the safety of the approach
Cardinal Principles: Power, Attitude, Configuration
Not inherently dangerous, but becomes dangerous when delayed or flown improperly
Delaying often stems from two sources:
Landing expectancy: Belief that conditions are not as threatening as they are, and the approach will end safely
Pride: Mistaken belief that a go around is an admission of failure
Decision making
Maintain a stabilized approach
Momentary deviations from speed, glidepath and centerline are acceptable
Set altitude gates
If you don’t meet set criteria at specified altitudes, go-around (no questions asked)
Ex. Stable and configured for landing at 500’
In an emergency, you may have to choose between going around or continuing to land
Go Around Considerations
There are situations that can be handled better airborne than on the ground
Ex: landing gear. Go around and attempt to solve the problem airborne
Continuing to Land Considerations
There are situations that can be better handled by landing instead of going around
Ex: emergencies that can affect the airplane’s ability to fly, or fire
Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO) 							AI.VII.B.R3b
Basics
Operations that include landing and holding short of an intersecting runway, taxiway, or other point
Pilot Responsibilities
Preflight Planning
Become familiar with all LAHSO information at the destination
Landing performance – knowledge of landing data allows for a quick decision
PIC has the final authority to accept or decline any LAHSO clearance
Once accepted, a LAHSO clearance must be adhered to, unless otherwise coordinated
Does not prevent a rejected landing
Full readback of LAHSO clearance is required
Situational Awareness
Have current airport information (diagram, LAHSO procedures, etc.)
To conduct LAHSO operations properly, understand the following:
Landing distance available
Be advised by ATC as to why LAHSO are being conducted
Advise if you cannot accept LAHSO
LAHSO/airport signs, markings, lights
Not authorized for solo student pilots
Air carriers are often not authorized LAHSO if the other aircraft is GA
Generally, not authorized at night
Not authorized on wet runways
LAHSO Minimums
Basic VFR: 1,000’ ceiling & 3 SM visibility
Wind Shear 											AI.VII.B.R2b
What is it?
A sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or direction over a very small area
While wind shear can occur at any altitude, low-level wind shear is especially hazardous
Why is it dangerous?
Violent updrafts and downdrafts (up to 6,000 fpm) / abrupt changes to horizontal movement
Rapid changes in performance (tailwind shears to headwind, or headwind to tailwind)
Microbursts
Most severe type of wind shear
Characteristics
1-2 miles across
Lifespan of 5-15 mins.
Strong downdrafts
Strong turbulence
Headwind gains/losses of 30-90 knots
Indications
Visual – Intense rain shaft at the surface, but virga at cloud base; ring of blowing dust
Alerting Systems
LLWAS-NE, TDWR, and ASR-9 WSP systems installed at major airports
Many airports, especially smaller airports, have no wind shear systems
Handling Wind Shear
If possible, avoid it
Never conduct traffic pattern operations near an active thunderstorm
LLWAS (Low Level Wind Shear Alerting System) can warn of windshear
PIREPS
Approach into Wind Shear
Follow the POH procedures. If none, general techniques include:
Higher power and faster approach speed (add ½ the gust factor to approach speed)
Stay as high as feasible until necessary to descend
Go around at the first sign of an unexpected pitch or airspeed change
It is important to get FULL power and get the plane climbing
If the aircraft is descending toward the ground, ensure max power, increase pitch attitude as far as possible without stalling the airplane
Intent is to keep flying as long as possible in hope of exiting the shear
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28) Ch. 22 pgs. 7-18 for more details
Wake Turbulence 										AI.VII.B.R2d
What is it?
Difference between the high and low pressure below/above the wing causes the air to move outward, upward and around the wingtips, leading to counter rotating vortices
All aircraft generate wake turbulence during flight
The larger the aircraft, the stronger the vortices
Vortices are strongest when the pressure differential is greatest (heavy, clean, slow)
Why is it Dangerous?
Rolling moments can exceed control authority and/or damage the aircraft
Wake turbulence can be encountered in any phase of flight (usually strongest at departure)
Vortex Behavior
Vortices are generated when an aircraft leaves the ground until it touches down
Remain about a wingspan apart and drift with wind at altitudes > a wingspan above the ground
Sink at a rate of several hundred FPM, slowing descent and diminishing in strength over time
When close to the ground (100-200’), they tend to move laterally at 2-3 knots
A crosswind decreases lateral movement of upwind vortex, increases downwind vortex
Light quartering tailwind can result in vortices along final approach centerline
Avoidance Procedures - Landing after a large aircraft:
On the same Runway
Stay at/above their approach path & land beyond their touchdown point (Figure A)
On a Parallel Runway (< 2,500’ away)
Consider drift & stay at/above their flight path, note touchdown point (Figure B)
On a Crossing Runway
Cross above their flight path (Figure C)
Departing on the same Runway
Land prior to their rotation point
Departing a Crossing Runway: Note their rotation point, if that point is past the intersection, land prior to the intersection
If they rotate prior to the intersection, avoid flight below their flight path
Abandon the approach unless a landing is ensured well before reaching the intersection
Executing a Low Approach, Missed Approach, or Touch-and-Go
Wait at least 2 minutes prior to landing
Distractions, Task Prioritization, SA 								AI.VII.B.R6
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop
Sterile flight deck during taxi, takeoff, and climb as well as descent and landing
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, especially in the traffic pattern
Maintain SA
Know where you are, what’s coming next, and stay ahead of the airplane
Be aware of other traffic. Build a 3d picture based on what you see, and hear on the radio
If SA or orientation is lost, admit it, and fix it
Disorientation: Get the aircraft to a safe attitude, airspeed, and altitude
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention full more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
If tasks are piling up, “Attack the closest alligator” – Deal with the most pressing problem
Safety is the number one priority - Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Low Altitude Maneuvering 									AI.VII.B.R5
A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially when slow, can result in a stall or loss of control close to the ground
Low Altitude Stall/Spin
A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
If you get any indication of a stall at low level, recover, and climb to a safe altitude
Spin
A spin is a result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Recover at the first sign of a stall
Maintain coordination
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Recovery (PARE)
Power - Idle
Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
Once the spin stops, neutralize the rudder & raise the nose, being careful not to stall again
Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries, follow the POH procedures
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) - AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range
Recommendations:
Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC
Know and fly above minimum published safe altitudes
If IFR, fly published procedures
Verify proper altitude, especially at night or overwater, through use of a correctly set altimeter
Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances
Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation
Don't operate below minimum safe altitudes if uncertain of position or ATC clearance
Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts and all available information
Use appropriate checklists
Know your aircraft and its equipment
Collision Hazards 										AI.VII.B.R4
Collision Avoidance
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Clearing Procedures
Descending: Execute gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Pattern: Scan for other traffic, enter traffic pattern at pattern altitude
Approach: Clear the runway
Uncontrolled Fields: Be conservative with spacing during takeoff, landing, and in the pattern
Clearly communicate intentions & location at uncontrolled fields
Operation Lights On (voluntary FAA safety program )
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging:
Same Category: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final approach have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Be aware of terrain that could cause a hazard during the climb or descent into the airfield
Study charts and use maximum elevation figures (MEFs) and other data
Day vs Night flying over terrain
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strikes
Many structures can significantly affect safety below 500’ AGL and particularly below 200’ AGL
Obstacles can be found in the NOTAMs, and the Terminal Procedures (IFR document)
< 200’ AGL are unmarked/lighted power lines, antenna towers, etc.
Antenna Towers: Numerous antennas extend over 1,000’-2,000’ AGL
Most are supported by guy wires which can extend 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires: Wires and lines span runway departures and landmarks pilots frequently follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc. (may not be lit)
Airport Surface
Be alert for vehicles, persons, wildlife, or anything that could cause a hazard
Reject or delay takeoff, as required. Go around if landing
Scan vigilantly during taxi for aircraft and obstacles - If unsure of clearance, stop until you’re sure
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

WHAT
A normal approach and landing involves the use of procedures for what is considered a normal situation – engine power is available, the wind is light, or the final approach is made directly into the wind, the final approach path has no obstacles, and the landing surface is firm and of ample length to gradually bring the plane to a stop.

It’s really a good skill to have when we decide we want to land the plane. Not only that, but the factors involved, and procedures used also have applications to the other-than-normal approaches and landings we’ll learn later.

Started approximately 10’ to 20’ above the ground (varies between aircraft and rate of descent)
Power is reduced to idle and back elevator is applied to gradually increase pitch attitude
With the power at idle, airspeed is decreasing – As airspeed decreases, the pilot increases the angle of attack which momentarily increases lift and decreases the rate of descent
Airspeed will continue to decrease causing lift to continue to decrease
Airspeed is being decreased to touchdown speed, while lift is being controlled with back pressure so that the airplane will settle gently onto the runway
Rate of the Roundout – Varies with the height above the ground, the rate of descent, and the pitch attitude
High Roundout: Executed slower to allow the plane to descend
