paragraphs.text: VII.M. Slip to a Landing
Introduction
How
What is a Slip? 											AI.VII.M.K1
Overview
A slip is a combination of forward and sideward movement
The plane is flying sideways, resulting in a change in the direction the relative wind strikes the plane
Characterized by an increase in drag, along with a decrease in climb, cruise & glide performance
Positive Static Stability
Most planes have positive static directional stability (innate tendency to compensate for slips)
Requires deliberate cross-controlled ailerons and rudder throughout the maneuver
Two Types of Slips
Forward Slip: Used to steepen the descent angle without excessively increasing airspeed
Especially useful in forced landings and when obstacles must be cleared during the approach
One wing is lowered, while yawing the opposite direction (angled to original path)
The amount of slip (& sink rate) is determined by amount of bank
Sideslip: Used in crosswind landings to keep aligned with the centerline & prevent drift
Longitudinal axis remains parallel to the original flight path
Lower one wing into the wind & use opposite rudder to keep the longitudinal axis aligned with the centerline
Aileron corrects for wind; rudder keeps the airplane aligned with the centerline
Touchdown occurs on the upwind wheel, then the downwind wheel, then the nose wheel
Practical Slip Limit
Amount of slip is limited by the amount of rudder available
There’s a point where full rudder is needed to maintain heading even though ailerons can steepen bank
Practical Slip Limit: Any additional bank results in a turn even though full opposite rudder is applied
If there is a need to descend more rapidly, lowering the nose will increase the descent and airspeed
Increased airspeed increases rudder effectiveness, permitting a steeper slip
Conversely, when the nose is raised, rudder effectiveness decreases, and bank must be reduced
RM: Forward Slip Operations 								AI.VII.M.R7
Airspeed Indicator Errors
Airspeed indicators may have considerable error when in a slip
A change in either the static or ram pressure will result in a change in the airspeed
Static Error Example – Static port on the left side, and pilot enters a slip to the left
Static port now receives some amount of ram air pressure
Static pressure increases, and for arguments sake, the pitot pressure remains the same
Results in a lower indicated airspeed than what is being flown
Pitot Error Example
Pitot tube is no longer directly into the relative wind, reducing ram air/airspeed accuracy
Reference the POH, be aware of any airspeed indicator errors / limitations
The pilot must be aware of the potential for errors and recognize a properly performed slip by the:
Airplane attitude, sound of the airflow, and feel of the flight controls
Stalls in a Slip
If improperly flown, a cross-controlled stall can be entered in a slip
Can be extremely hazardous close to the ground – some aircraft tend to roll over
Displays little of the yawing tendency that causes a skidding stall to develop into a spin
Stall characteristics may be improved, the plane may even tend to roll to a wings level attitude
In a slip, the raised wing has a higher angle of attack than the low wing and will stall first
Often the stall of the high wing first will reduce the bank angle, preventing a further stall
Tail Stalls with Flaps
Not recommended to slip some aircraft with flaps extended, because it can result in a tail stall
Generally, having the flaps extended at high AOAs can blank out the relative wind over the horizontal stabilizer and result in a tail stall (may not be possible to recover)
Follow the manufacturer’s recommendations, and remove the slip at any indication of stall
Fuel Flow
In uncoordinated flight forces may pull fuel away from the fuel lines
Potential to cause fuel starvation and engine stoppage
Risk is greatest when fuel levels are low
Remove the slip at any indication of engine coughing or roughness
Performing the Forward Slip 					AI.VII.M.K1, AI.VII.M.K2, AI.VII.M.K4
Setup & Configuration
Checklists should be used as normal
The airplane will have to be established higher on final
Reduce power to idle (there is no logic in slipping to lose altitude with power)
Extend the flaps as necessary
Entry
The wing on the side toward which the slip is to be made should be lowered with the ailerons
Slip into the wind if a crosswind exists
Simultaneously yaw the nose the opposite direction so the plane is at an angle to the original flight path
The amount of yaw is such that the ground track is maintained
Raise the nose to prevent the airspeed from increasing
RM: Stabilized Approach 									AI.VII.M.R9
Rate of Descent
The amount of slip, and therefore sink rate, is determined by bank (more bank = more sink)
For maximum descent, use full rudder and adjust the aileron to maintain ground track
Pitch Attitude – Smoothly adjust pitch to maintain the desired approach speed
Precise Ground Track
Yaw the nose to the extent required to maintain ground track
If rudder is constant, the pilot can also adjust bank to maintain desired ground track
Increased Crosscheck – Crosscheck needs to accelerate during a slip
Stable is safe - Excessive swings in descent rates, airspeed, or ground track is unsafe
Remove the slip and go around if unstable
Discontinuing a Forward Slip
Level the wings and simultaneously release rudder pressure while readjusting the pitch attitude
Recovery should be smooth and controlled – no abrupt movements
RM: Touching down in a forward slip could be hazardous to the pilot and aircraft 		AI.VII.M.R8
Never land in a forward slip. Can impose severe side loads on the gear
Performing the Sideslip 						AI.VII.M.K1, AI.VII.M.K2, AI.VII.M.K4
Entering
Checklists - Use as normal
Configuration – Normal landing configuration, unless specified otherwise
Maintain power setting
Not intended to increase sink as in a forward slip, therefore power is maintained
Always keep one hand on the throttle (within reason)
Extend flaps as necessary
Entry
Lower the upwind wing into the wind and apply just enough opposite rudder to prevent a turn
Aileron is used to keep the aircraft centered on the runway centerline
Rudder is used to keep the nose of the aircraft aligned with the runway
The amount of slip is determined by the strength of the crosswind
The stronger the crosswind, steeper the bank angle required to stay centered
As bank increases, additional opposite rudder is required to stay aligned with the centerline
The nose of the airplane should be raised slightly to prevent airspeed from increasing
RM: Crosswind Limits 									AI.VII.M.R2a
At some amount of crosswind, full rudder is required to maintain centerline alignment
Any additional crosswind will exceed the airplane’s ability to safely land
This is why there are crosswind limits in the aircraft POH
Forward Slip to a Sideslip
The pilot will have to transition from a forward slip to a sideslip
Situation where a high rate of descent is required and a landing with a crosswind
The forward slip should be performed into the wind
On a normal glidepath, remove the forward slip, maintain airspeed/path, and establish a sideslip
Stabilized Approach
Energy Management
Reference Appendix A. Energy Management as needed for more energy management concepts
Corresponding slides can be found in the slide’s appendix
Select an Aim Point; use pitch and power to maintain a stable approach to the aim point
Precise Ground Track (while maintaining aim point/glidepath)
Use bank to counter the crosswind and rudder to align with the centerline
As conditions vary (gusts, etc.) adjust aileron and rudder
Go Around if Unstable - Excessive swings in descent, airspeed, and ground track can be hazardous
Landing in a Sideslip 										AI.VII.M.R2a
Maintain the slip during landing - Removing the sideslip over the runway will result in drifting
Drift can result in severe side loads, or even being pushed off the runway entirely
The plane will touchdown on the upwind main first, then the downwind main, then the nosewheel
Maintain directional control after touchdown
Directional control must be maintained to counter the crosswind after landing
Keep the aileron into the wind. As speed decreases, increase aileron deflection
RM: Runway Selection 									AI.VII.M.R1
Limitations
Chapter 2 of the POH – Review applicable limitations
Can include: Max weights, CG limitations, Crosswind/Tailwind restrictions, Runway length/width limitations, flap & gear extension speeds, stalls speeds, and more
Wind
Preferred to land with a headwind – reduces landing distance
RM: Tailwinds increase ground speed/ground roll (verify limitations) 			AI.VII.M.R2c
(RM: Effects of tailwind)
RM: Ensure any crosswind is within limits (personal & POH) (RM: Effects of crosswind)	AI.VII.M.R2a
Aircraft Performance
Atmospheric Pressure
Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded, affecting density
Air density affects performance - As density increases, performance increases & vice versa
What Changes Air Density (DA)? - Barometric Pressure, Temperature, Altitude, and Humidity
Density varies directly with pressure - As pressure increases, density increases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with temperature – As temp increases, density decreases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with altitude - As altitude increases, density decreases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with humidity – As humidity increases, density decreases and vice versa
How it affects Performance
As the air becomes less dense, it reduces:
Power, since the engine takes in less air
Thrust, since the propeller is less efficient in thin air (less air is being moved for every rotation)
Lift, because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils
Density Altitude & Landing
Affects climb capability in the case of a go-around
Higher density altitude = higher true airspeed which increases the landing roll
RM: Runway Characteristics 									AI.VII.M.R2e
Surface: More friction associated with softer surfaces decreases landing roll
Gradient: Down sloping runway increases landing roll
Condition : Dry, wet, snow, ice, etc. affect braking effectiveness
Available Distance: Compare to the required landing distance
Performance Charts
Take into account all of the above information, and more (weight, configuration, etc.)
Verify required landing distance based on the specific conditions (atmospheric, airplane, etc.)
Pilot Capability: Strictly adhere to personal minimums – Ensure proficiency and safety
Runway Selection
Combination of all the above factors
Generally, boils down to Limitations + Performance + Personal Minimums
Common Errors 										AI.VII.M.K5
Incorrect pitch adjustments that result in poor airspeed control
Reacting to erroneous airspeed indications
Using excess power while trying to lose altitude
A slip in the same direction as any crosswind
Poor glidepath control
Late transition to a sideslip during landing with crosswinds
Landing without the longitudinal axis parallel to runway and/or off centerline
RM: Hazards & Emergencies
Rejected Landing & Go-Around 								AI.VII.M.R3a
When to Go-Around
When it’s hazardous to continue or if you’re ever in doubt of the safety of the approach
Cardinal Principles: Power, Attitude, Configuration
Not inherently dangerous, but becomes dangerous when delayed or flown improperly
Delaying often stems from two sources:
Landing expectancy: Belief that conditions are not as threatening as they are, and the approach will end safely
Pride: Mistaken belief that a go around is an admission of failure
Decision making
Maintain a stabilized approach
Momentary deviations from speed, glidepath and centerline are acceptable
Set Altitude Gates: If you don’t meet set criteria at set altitudes, go-around, no questions asked
Ex. Stable and configured for landing at 500’
In an emergency, you may have to choose between going around or continuing to land
Go Around Considerations
There are situations that can be handled better airborne than on the ground
Ex: landing gear. Go around and attempt to solve the problem airborne
Continuing to Land Considerations
There are situations that can be better handled by landing instead of going around
Ex: emergencies that can affect the airplane’s ability to fly, or fire
Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO) 							AI.VII.M.R3b
Basics
Operations that include landing and holding short of an intersecting runway, taxiway, or other point
Pilot Responsibilities
Preflight Planning
Become familiar with all LAHSO information at the destination
Landing performance – knowledge of landing data allows for a quick decision
PIC has the final authority to accept or decline any LAHSO clearance
Once accepted, a LAHSO clearance must be adhered to, unless otherwise coordinated
Does not prevent a rejected landing
Full readback of LAHSO clearance is required
Situational Awareness
Have current airport information (diagram, LAHSO procedures, etc.)
To conduct LAHSO operations properly, understand the following:
Landing distance available
Be advised by ATC as to why LAHSO are being conducted
Advise if you cannot accept LAHSO
LAHSO/airport signs, markings, lights
Not authorized for solo student pilots
Air carriers are often not authorized LAHSO if the other aircraft is GA
Generally, not authorized at night
Not authorized on wet runways
LAHSO Minimums
Basic VFR: 1,000’ ceiling & 3 SM visibility
Wind Shear 											AI.VII.M.R2b
What is it?
A sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or direction over a very small area
While wind shear can occur at any altitude, low-level wind shear is especially hazardous
Why is it dangerous?
Violent updrafts and downdrafts (up to 6,000 fpm) / abrupt changes to horizontal movement
Rapid changes in performance (tailwind shears to headwind, or headwind to tailwind)
Microbursts
Most severe type of wind shear
Characteristics
1-2 miles across
Lifespan of 5-15 mins.
Strong downdrafts
Strong turbulence
Headwind gains/losses of 30-90 knots
Indications
Visual – Intense rain shaft at the surface, but virga at cloud base; ring of blowing dust
Alerting Systems
LLWAS-NE, TDWR, and ASR-9 WSP systems installed at major airports
Many airports, especially smaller airports, have no wind shear systems
Handling Wind Shear
If possible, avoid it
Never conduct traffic pattern operations near an active thunderstorm
LLWAS (Low Level Wind Shear Alerting System) can warn of windshear
PIREPS
Approach into Wind Shear
Follow POH procedures. If none, general techniques include:
Higher power and faster approach speed (add ½ the gust factor to approach speed)
Stay as high as feasible until necessary to descend
Go around at the first sign of an unexpected pitch or airspeed change
It is important to get FULL power and get the plane climbing
If the aircraft is descending toward the ground, ensure max power, increase pitch attitude as far as possible without stalling the airplane
Intent is to keep flying as long as possible in hope of exiting the shear
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28) Ch. 22 pgs. 7-18 for more details
Wake Turbulence 										AI.VII.M.R2d
What is it?
Difference between the high and low pressure below/above the wing causes the air to move outward, upward and around the wingtips, leading to counter rotating vortices
All aircraft generate wake turbulence during flight
The larger the aircraft, the stronger the vortices
Vortices are strongest when the pressure differential is greatest (heavy, clean, slow)
Why is it Dangerous?
Rolling moments can exceed control authority and/or damage the aircraft
Wake turbulence can be encountered in any phase of flight (usually strongest at departure)
Vortex Behavior
Vortices are generated when an aircraft leaves the ground until it touches down
Remain about a wingspan apart and drift with wind at altitudes > a wingspan above the ground
Sink at a rate of several hundred FPM, slowing descent and diminishing in strength over time
When close to the ground (100-200’), they tend to move laterally at 2-3 knots
A crosswind decreases lateral movement of upwind vortex, increases downwind vortex
Light quartering tailwind can result in vortices along final approach centerline
Avoidance Procedures - Landing after a large aircraft:
On the same Runway
Stay at/above their approach path & land beyond their touchdown point (Figure A)
On a Parallel Runway (< 2,500’ away)
Consider drift & stay at/above their flight path, note touchdown point (Figure B)
On a Crossing Runway
Cross above their flight path (Figure C)
Departing on the same Runway
Land prior to their rotation point
Departing a Crossing Runway: Note their rotation point, if that point is past the intersection, land prior to the intersection
If they rotate prior to the intersection, avoid flight below their flight path
Abandon the approach unless a landing is ensured well before reaching the intersection
Executing a Low Approach, Missed Approach, or Touch-and-Go
Wait at least 2 minutes prior to landing
Distractions, Task Prioritization, SA 								AI.VII.M.R6
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop
Sterile flight deck during taxi, takeoff, and climb as well as descent and landing
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, especially in the pattern
Maintain SA
Know where you are, what’s coming next, and stay ahead of the airplane
Be aware of other traffic. Build a 3d picture based on what you see, and hear on the radio
If SA or orientation is lost, admit it, and fix it
Disorientation: Get the aircraft to a safe attitude, airspeed, and altitude
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention full more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
If tasks are piling up, “Attack the closest alligator” – Deal with the most pressing problem
Safety is the number one priority - Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Low Altitude Maneuvering 									AI.VII.M.R5
A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially if slow, can result in a stall/loss of control near the ground
Low Altitude Stall/Spin
A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
If you get any indication of a stall at low level, recover, and climb to a safe altitude
Spin
A spin is a result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Recover at the first sign of a stall
Maintain coordination
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Recovery (PARE)
Power - Idle
Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
Once the spin stops, neutralize the rudder & raise the nose, being careful not to stall again
Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries, follow the POH procedures
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) - AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range
Recommendations:
Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC
Know and fly above minimum published safe altitudes
If IFR, fly published procedures
Verify proper altitude, especially at night or overwater, through use of a correctly set altimeter
Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances
Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation
Don't operate below minimum safe altitudes if uncertain of position or ATC clearance
Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts, appropriate checklists, and know your aircraft and its equipment
Collision Hazards 										AI.VII.M.R4
Collision Avoidance
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Clearing Procedures
Descending: Execute gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Pattern: Scan for other traffic, enter traffic pattern at pattern altitude
Approach: Clear the runway
Uncontrolled Fields: Be conservative with spacing during takeoff, landing, and in the pattern
Clearly communicate intentions & location at uncontrolled fields
Operation Lights On (voluntary FAA safety program )
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging:
Same Category: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final approach have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Be aware of terrain that could cause a hazard during the climb or descent into the airfield
Study charts and use maximum elevation figures (MEFs) and other data
Day vs Night flying over terrain
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strikes
Many structures can significantly affect safety below 500’ AGL and particularly below 200’ AGL
Obstacles can be found in the NOTAMs, and the Terminal Procedures (IFR document)
< 200’ AGL are unmarked/lighted power lines, antenna towers, etc.
Antenna Towers: Numerous antennas extend over 1,000’-2,000’ AGL
Most are supported by guy wires which can extend 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires: Wires and lines span runway departures and landmarks pilots frequently follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc. (may not be lit)
Airport Surface
Be alert for vehicles, persons, wildlife, or anything that could cause a hazard
Reject or delay takeoff, as required. Go around if landing
Scan vigilantly during taxi for aircraft and obstacles - If unsure of clearance, stop until you’re sure
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

VII.M. Slip to a Landing
Introduction
How
What is a Slip? 											AI.VII.M.K1
Overview
A slip is a combination of forward and sideward movement
The plane is flying sideways, resulting in a change in the direction the relative wind strikes the plane
Characterized by an increase in drag, along with a decrease in climb, cruise & glide performance
Positive Static Stability
Most planes have positive static directional stability (innate tendency to compensate for slips)
Requires deliberate cross-controlled ailerons and rudder throughout the maneuver
Two Types of Slips
Forward Slip: Used to steepen the descent angle without excessively increasing airspeed
Especially useful in forced landings and when obstacles must be cleared during the approach
One wing is lowered, while yawing the opposite direction (angled to original path)
The amount of slip (& sink rate) is determined by amount of bank
Sideslip: Used in crosswind landings to keep aligned with the centerline & prevent drift
Longitudinal axis remains parallel to the original flight path
Lower one wing into the wind & use opposite rudder to keep the longitudinal axis aligned with the centerline
Aileron corrects for wind; rudder keeps the airplane aligned with the centerline
Touchdown occurs on the upwind wheel, then the downwind wheel, then the nose wheel
Practical Slip Limit
Amount of slip is limited by the amount of rudder available
There’s a point where full rudder is needed to maintain heading even though ailerons can steepen bank
Practical Slip Limit: Any additional bank results in a turn even though full opposite rudder is applied
If there is a need to descend more rapidly, lowering the nose will increase the descent and airspeed
Increased airspeed increases rudder effectiveness, permitting a steeper slip
Conversely, when the nose is raised, rudder effectiveness decreases, and bank must be reduced
RM: Forward Slip Operations 								AI.VII.M.R7
Airspeed Indicator Errors
Airspeed indicators may have considerable error when in a slip
A change in either the static or ram pressure will result in a change in the airspeed
Static Error Example – Static port on the left side, and pilot enters a slip to the left
Static port now receives some amount of ram air pressure
Static pressure increases, and for arguments sake, the pitot pressure remains the same
Results in a lower indicated airspeed than what is being flown
Pitot Error Example
Pitot tube is no longer directly into the relative wind, reducing ram air/airspeed accuracy
Reference the POH, be aware of any airspeed indicator errors / limitations
The pilot must be aware of the potential for errors and recognize a properly performed slip by the:
Airplane attitude, sound of the airflow, and feel of the flight controls
Stalls in a Slip
If improperly flown, a cross-controlled stall can be entered in a slip
Can be extremely hazardous close to the ground – some aircraft tend to roll over
Displays little of the yawing tendency that causes a skidding stall to develop into a spin
Stall characteristics may be improved, the plane may even tend to roll to a wings level attitude
In a slip, the raised wing has a higher angle of attack than the low wing and will stall first
Often the stall of the high wing first will reduce the bank angle, preventing a further stall
Tail Stalls with Flaps
Not recommended to slip some aircraft with flaps extended, because it can result in a tail stall
Generally, having the flaps extended at high AOAs can blank out the relative wind over the horizontal stabilizer and result in a tail stall (may not be possible to recover)
Follow the manufacturer’s recommendations, and remove the slip at any indication of stall
Fuel Flow
In uncoordinated flight forces may pull fuel away from the fuel lines
Potential to cause fuel starvation and engine stoppage
Risk is greatest when fuel levels are low
Remove the slip at any indication of engine coughing or roughness
Performing the Forward Slip 					AI.VII.M.K1, AI.VII.M.K2, AI.VII.M.K4
Setup & Configuration
Checklists should be used as normal
The airplane will have to be established higher on final
Reduce power to idle (there is no logic in slipping to lose altitude with power)
Extend the flaps as necessary
Entry
The wing on the side toward which the slip is to be made should be lowered with the ailerons
Slip into the wind if a crosswind exists
Simultaneously yaw the nose the opposite direction so the plane is at an angle to the original flight path
The amount of yaw is such that the ground track is maintained
Raise the nose to prevent the airspeed from increasing
RM: Stabilized Approach 									AI.VII.M.R9
Rate of Descent
The amount of slip, and therefore sink rate, is determined by bank (more bank = more sink)
For maximum descent, use full rudder and adjust the aileron to maintain ground track
Pitch Attitude – Smoothly adjust pitch to maintain the desired approach speed
Precise Ground Track
Yaw the nose to the extent required to maintain ground track
If rudder is constant, the pilot can also adjust bank to maintain desired ground track
Increased Crosscheck – Crosscheck needs to accelerate during a slip
Stable is safe - Excessive swings in descent rates, airspeed, or ground track is unsafe
Remove the slip and go around if unstable
Discontinuing a Forward Slip
Level the wings and simultaneously release rudder pressure while readjusting the pitch attitude
Recovery should be smooth and controlled – no abrupt movements
RM: Touching down in a forward slip could be hazardous to the pilot and aircraft 		AI.VII.M.R8
Never land in a forward slip. Can impose severe side loads on the gear
Performing the Sideslip 						AI.VII.M.K1, AI.VII.M.K2, AI.VII.M.K4
Entering
Checklists - Use as normal
Configuration – Normal landing configuration, unless specified otherwise
Maintain power setting
Not intended to increase sink as in a forward slip, therefore power is maintained
Always keep one hand on the throttle (within reason)
Extend flaps as necessary
Entry
Lower the upwind wing into the wind and apply just enough opposite rudder to prevent a turn
Aileron is used to keep the aircraft centered on the runway centerline
Rudder is used to keep the nose of the aircraft aligned with the runway
The amount of slip is determined by the strength of the crosswind
The stronger the crosswind, steeper the bank angle required to stay centered
As bank increases, additional opposite rudder is required to stay aligned with the centerline
The nose of the airplane should be raised slightly to prevent airspeed from increasing
RM: Crosswind Limits 									AI.VII.M.R2a
At some amount of crosswind, full rudder is required to maintain centerline alignment
Any additional crosswind will exceed the airplane’s ability to safely land
This is why there are crosswind limits in the aircraft POH
Forward Slip to a Sideslip
The pilot will have to transition from a forward slip to a sideslip
Situation where a high rate of descent is required and a landing with a crosswind
The forward slip should be performed into the wind
On a normal glidepath, remove the forward slip, maintain airspeed/path, and establish a sideslip
Stabilized Approach
Energy Management
Reference Appendix A. Energy Management as needed for more energy management concepts
Corresponding slides can be found in the slide’s appendix
Select an Aim Point; use pitch and power to maintain a stable approach to the aim point
Precise Ground Track (while maintaining aim point/glidepath)
Use bank to counter the crosswind and rudder to align with the centerline
As conditions vary (gusts, etc.) adjust aileron and rudder
Go Around if Unstable - Excessive swings in descent, airspeed, and ground track can be hazardous
Landing in a Sideslip 										AI.VII.M.R2a
Maintain the slip during landing - Removing the sideslip over the runway will result in drifting
Drift can result in severe side loads, or even being pushed off the runway entirely
The plane will touchdown on the upwind main first, then the downwind main, then the nosewheel
Maintain directional control after touchdown
Directional control must be maintained to counter the crosswind after landing
Keep the aileron into the wind. As speed decreases, increase aileron deflection
RM: Runway Selection 									AI.VII.M.R1
Limitations
Chapter 2 of the POH – Review applicable limitations
Can include: Max weights, CG limitations, Crosswind/Tailwind restrictions, Runway length/width limitations, flap & gear extension speeds, stalls speeds, and more
Wind
Preferred to land with a headwind – reduces landing distance
RM: Tailwinds increase ground speed/ground roll (verify limitations) 			AI.VII.M.R2c
(RM: Effects of tailwind)
RM: Ensure any crosswind is within limits (personal & POH) (RM: Effects of crosswind)	AI.VII.M.R2a
Aircraft Performance
Atmospheric Pressure
Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded, affecting density
Air density affects performance - As density increases, performance increases & vice versa
What Changes Air Density (DA)? - Barometric Pressure, Temperature, Altitude, and Humidity
Density varies directly with pressure - As pressure increases, density increases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with temperature – As temp increases, density decreases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with altitude - As altitude increases, density decreases and vice versa
Density varies inversely with humidity – As humidity increases, density decreases and vice versa
How it affects Performance
As the air becomes less dense, it reduces:
Power, since the engine takes in less air
Thrust, since the propeller is less efficient in thin air (less air is being moved for every rotation)
Lift, because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils
Density Altitude & Landing
Affects climb capability in the case of a go-around
Higher density altitude = higher true airspeed which increases the landing roll
RM: Runway Characteristics 									AI.VII.M.R2e
Surface: More friction associated with softer surfaces decreases landing roll
Gradient: Down sloping runway increases landing roll
Condition : Dry, wet, snow, ice, etc. affect braking effectiveness
Available Distance: Compare to the required landing distance
Performance Charts
Take into account all of the above information, and more (weight, configuration, etc.)
Verify required landing distance based on the specific conditions (atmospheric, airplane, etc.)
Pilot Capability: Strictly adhere to personal minimums – Ensure proficiency and safety
Runway Selection
Combination of all the above factors
Generally, boils down to Limitations + Performance + Personal Minimums
Common Errors 										AI.VII.M.K5
Incorrect pitch adjustments that result in poor airspeed control
Reacting to erroneous airspeed indications
Using excess power while trying to lose altitude
A slip in the same direction as any crosswind
Poor glidepath control
Late transition to a sideslip during landing with crosswinds
Landing without the longitudinal axis parallel to runway and/or off centerline
RM: Hazards & Emergencies
Rejected Landing & Go-Around 								AI.VII.M.R3a
When to Go-Around
When it’s hazardous to continue or if you’re ever in doubt of the safety of the approach
Cardinal Principles: Power, Attitude, Configuration
Not inherently dangerous, but becomes dangerous when delayed or flown improperly
Delaying often stems from two sources:
Landing expectancy: Belief that conditions are not as threatening as they are, and the approach will end safely
Pride: Mistaken belief that a go around is an admission of failure
Decision making
Maintain a stabilized approach
Momentary deviations from speed, glidepath and centerline are acceptable
Set Altitude Gates: If you don’t meet set criteria at set altitudes, go-around, no questions asked
Ex. Stable and configured for landing at 500’
In an emergency, you may have to choose between going around or continuing to land
Go Around Considerations
There are situations that can be handled better airborne than on the ground
Ex: landing gear. Go around and attempt to solve the problem airborne
Continuing to Land Considerations
There are situations that can be better handled by landing instead of going around
Ex: emergencies that can affect the airplane’s ability to fly, or fire
Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO) 							AI.VII.M.R3b
Basics
Operations that include landing and holding short of an intersecting runway, taxiway, or other point
Pilot Responsibilities
Preflight Planning
Become familiar with all LAHSO information at the destination
Landing performance – knowledge of landing data allows for a quick decision
PIC has the final authority to accept or decline any LAHSO clearance
Once accepted, a LAHSO clearance must be adhered to, unless otherwise coordinated
Does not prevent a rejected landing
Full readback of LAHSO clearance is required
Situational Awareness
Have current airport information (diagram, LAHSO procedures, etc.)
To conduct LAHSO operations properly, understand the following:
Landing distance available
Be advised by ATC as to why LAHSO are being conducted
Advise if you cannot accept LAHSO
LAHSO/airport signs, markings, lights
Not authorized for solo student pilots
Air carriers are often not authorized LAHSO if the other aircraft is GA
Generally, not authorized at night
Not authorized on wet runways
LAHSO Minimums
Basic VFR: 1,000’ ceiling & 3 SM visibility
Wind Shear 											AI.VII.M.R2b
What is it?
A sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or direction over a very small area
While wind shear can occur at any altitude, low-level wind shear is especially hazardous
Why is it dangerous?
Violent updrafts and downdrafts (up to 6,000 fpm) / abrupt changes to horizontal movement
Rapid changes in performance (tailwind shears to headwind, or headwind to tailwind)
Microbursts
Most severe type of wind shear
Characteristics
1-2 miles across
Lifespan of 5-15 mins.
Strong downdrafts
Strong turbulence
Headwind gains/losses of 30-90 knots
Indications
Visual – Intense rain shaft at the surface, but virga at cloud base; ring of blowing dust
Alerting Systems
LLWAS-NE, TDWR, and ASR-9 WSP systems installed at major airports
Many airports, especially smaller airports, have no wind shear systems
Handling Wind Shear
If possible, avoid it
Never conduct traffic pattern operations near an active thunderstorm
LLWAS (Low Level Wind Shear Alerting System) can warn of windshear
PIREPS
Approach into Wind Shear
Follow POH procedures. If none, general techniques include:
Higher power and faster approach speed (add ½ the gust factor to approach speed)
Stay as high as feasible until necessary to descend
Go around at the first sign of an unexpected pitch or airspeed change
It is important to get FULL power and get the plane climbing
If the aircraft is descending toward the ground, ensure max power, increase pitch attitude as far as possible without stalling the airplane
Intent is to keep flying as long as possible in hope of exiting the shear
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28) Ch. 22 pgs. 7-18 for more details
Wake Turbulence 										AI.VII.M.R2d
What is it?
Difference between the high and low pressure below/above the wing causes the air to move outward, upward and around the wingtips, leading to counter rotating vortices
All aircraft generate wake turbulence during flight
The larger the aircraft, the stronger the vortices
Vortices are strongest when the pressure differential is greatest (heavy, clean, slow)
Why is it Dangerous?
Rolling moments can exceed control authority and/or damage the aircraft
Wake turbulence can be encountered in any phase of flight (usually strongest at departure)
Vortex Behavior
Vortices are generated when an aircraft leaves the ground until it touches down
Remain about a wingspan apart and drift with wind at altitudes > a wingspan above the ground
Sink at a rate of several hundred FPM, slowing descent and diminishing in strength over time
When close to the ground (100-200’), they tend to move laterally at 2-3 knots
A crosswind decreases lateral movement of upwind vortex, increases downwind vortex
Light quartering tailwind can result in vortices along final approach centerline
Avoidance Procedures - Landing after a large aircraft:
On the same Runway
Stay at/above their approach path & land beyond their touchdown point (Figure A)
On a Parallel Runway (< 2,500’ away)
Consider drift & stay at/above their flight path, note touchdown point (Figure B)
On a Crossing Runway
Cross above their flight path (Figure C)
Departing on the same Runway
Land prior to their rotation point
Departing a Crossing Runway: Note their rotation point, if that point is past the intersection, land prior to the intersection
If they rotate prior to the intersection, avoid flight below their flight path
Abandon the approach unless a landing is ensured well before reaching the intersection
Executing a Low Approach, Missed Approach, or Touch-and-Go
Wait at least 2 minutes prior to landing
Distractions, Task Prioritization, SA 								AI.VII.M.R6
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop
Sterile flight deck during taxi, takeoff, and climb as well as descent and landing
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, especially in the pattern
Maintain SA
Know where you are, what’s coming next, and stay ahead of the airplane
Be aware of other traffic. Build a 3d picture based on what you see, and hear on the radio
If SA or orientation is lost, admit it, and fix it
Disorientation: Get the aircraft to a safe attitude, airspeed, and altitude
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
No one responsibility should take your full attention full more than a short period
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
If tasks are piling up, “Attack the closest alligator” – Deal with the most pressing problem
Safety is the number one priority - Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Low Altitude Maneuvering 									AI.VII.M.R5
A small problem at high altitude can quickly become a big problem at a low altitude
Quick, panicked maneuvers, especially if slow, can result in a stall/loss of control near the ground
Low Altitude Stall/Spin
A low altitude stall or spin can leave little to no recovery time
ALWAYS maintain coordination, and airspeed at low altitudes
If you get any indication of a stall at low level, recover, and climb to a safe altitude
Spin
A spin is a result of a stall + yaw
Prevention
Recover at the first sign of a stall
Maintain coordination
Do not use abrupt, excessive pressure inputs (especially back elevator pressure)
Recovery (PARE)
Power - Idle
Ailerons - Neutral
Rudder - Full rudder opposite the spin direction
Elevator - Brisk, positive forward pressure (nose down)
Once the spin stops, neutralize the rudder & raise the nose, being careful not to stall again
Different aircraft respond differently to spins and spin recoveries, follow the POH procedures
CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) - AC 61-134: General Aviation CFIT Awareness
The solution to combating CFIT accidents starts on the ground
Common themes include proper planning, good decision making, and being able to safely operate the aircraft throughout its entire operating range
Recommendations:
Non-instrument rated VFR pilots should not attempt to fly in IMC
Know and fly above minimum published safe altitudes
If IFR, fly published procedures
Verify proper altitude, especially at night or overwater, through use of a correctly set altimeter
Verify all ATC clearances. Question potentially hazardous clearances
Maintain situational awareness both vertically and horizontally
Comply with appropriate regulations for your specific operation
Don't operate below minimum safe altitudes if uncertain of position or ATC clearance
Be extra careful when operating in an area which you are not familiar
Use current charts, appropriate checklists, and know your aircraft and its equipment
Collision Hazards 										AI.VII.M.R4
Collision Avoidance
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Clearing Procedures
Descending: Execute gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Pattern: Scan for other traffic, enter traffic pattern at pattern altitude
Approach: Clear the runway
Uncontrolled Fields: Be conservative with spacing during takeoff, landing, and in the pattern
Clearly communicate intentions & location at uncontrolled fields
Operation Lights On (voluntary FAA safety program )
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging:
Same Category: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final approach have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Be aware of terrain that could cause a hazard during the climb or descent into the airfield
Study charts and use maximum elevation figures (MEFs) and other data
Day vs Night flying over terrain
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strikes
Many structures can significantly affect safety below 500’ AGL and particularly below 200’ AGL
Obstacles can be found in the NOTAMs, and the Terminal Procedures (IFR document)
< 200’ AGL are unmarked/lighted power lines, antenna towers, etc.
Antenna Towers: Numerous antennas extend over 1,000’-2,000’ AGL
Most are supported by guy wires which can extend 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires: Wires and lines span runway departures and landmarks pilots frequently follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc. (may not be lit)
Airport Surface
Be alert for vehicles, persons, wildlife, or anything that could cause a hazard
Reject or delay takeoff, as required. Go around if landing
Scan vigilantly during taxi for aircraft and obstacles - If unsure of clearance, stop until you’re sure
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

Introduction
How
Go-Around Situations
Unstable Approach (emphasize the importance of a stable approach)
Too low, too high, not aligned with the runway, airspeed control, rate of descent
A stable approach can be the most useful tool in avoiding a pilot induced go-around	AI.VII.N.K2
Energy Management
Set pitch and power, and make proactive adjustments to manage energy
Maintain a stable site picture to the aim point
Reference Appendix A. Energy Management as needed for more detailed energy management concepts - Corresponding slides can be found in the slide’s appendix
Wind correction on approach & landing 	 					AI.VII.N.K4
Crab to maintain track & transition to a sideslip when ready
Air traffic control requirements
Low approach only request, or told to go-around, etc.
Unexpected hazards on the runway (another airplane, vehicles, animals, etc.)
Runway incursion: Be prepared to go-around in case another aircraft enters the runway 	AI.VII.N.R9
Overtaking another airplane
Wind Shear/Wake Turbulence
Mechanical Failure (Ex: Gear issues)
Whenever safety dictates
RM: Making a Prompt Decision
A go-around is not inherently dangerous, but becomes dangerous when unnecessarily delayed or executed improperly
RM: Delaying a go-around tends to stem from two sources: 				AI.VII.N.R2
Landing Expectancy: Belief that conditions are not threatening, and the approach will end safely
Pride: Mistaken belief that the act of going around is an admission of failure
RM: Delayed Recognition of the Need to Go-Around 					AI.VII.N.R1
(RM: Delayed performance of a go-around at low altitude)
Set and maintain standard operating procedures (SOPs) & altitude gates
Outside of SOP at the altitude gate = go-around. Techniques will vary, but could include:
500’ – Configured, airspeed ±5 knots, bank < 15o, on the desired approach path
250’ – Same as 500’ but with crosswind corrections established
Specific, measurable criteria allow for a logical easy decision (no emotion or questions)
It is very important to make a prompt decision
The earlier a situation that warrants a go-around is recognized, the safer the maneuver will be
If there’s a question as to go-around or not, it’s usually safer/smarter to execute the go around
Don’t allow a situation to magnify. Don’t hesitate. Stick to your decision. Safety first, always!
Go-Around
Cardinal Principles – Power, Attitude, Configuration  					AI.VII.N.K1
RM: Power – the pilot’s first concern 							AI.VII.N.R3
The instant the pilot decides to go-around, apply max takeoff power smoothly / without hesitation
Inertia – it takes considerable power, as well as time, to redirect an airplane’s inertia
The downward inertia of the airplane must be slowed, stopped, then reversed
Newton’s 1st Law - A body in motion wants to stay in motion
Controlling Power – When takeoff power is applied:
The nose may rise rapidly (especially if trimmed up for landing)
Hold forward pressure to maintain a safe attitude
Trim roughly to relieve some of the control pressures (fine tune later)
The nose will veer left
Right rudder pressure is necessary to counteract the left turning tendencies
Attitude
Attitude is always critical when close to the ground
An attitude must be established to allow the plane to gain sufficient speed before climbing / turning
Establish power, stop the descent, and when able, pitch to climb at VY (VX, if obstacles)
“Rough trim” the plane - Quick relieving of the control pressures. Trim more precisely once stable
Controlling Pitch Attitude
Raising the nose too early / aggressively could result in stall
If slow, it may be necessary to lower the nose briefly to gain airspeed
Summary: Increase power to max, stop the descent, and when safe, pitch to climb at VY (or VX)
RM: Configuration – Cleaning up the Airplane						AI.VII.N.R4
1st Concern: Landing Flaps
Reduce drag to assist the airplane in climbing and accelerating
Retracting the flaps increments allows time for the airplane to accelerate
A sudden / complete flap retraction could result in a significant loss of lift
2nd Concern: Gear (if retractable)
After a controlled, positive rate of climb is established, the gear can be retracted
3rd Concern: Takeoff Flaps
At this point, treat the situation like a normal takeoff
Retract the flaps as you normally would (safe airspeed and altitude)
Flaps Before Gear
Reduces the most drag immediately – full flaps tend to produce more drag than landing gear
If the airplane inadvertently touches down it is desirable to still have the gear down and locked
Climb Out
The majority of go-around climb outs will be identical to a normal takeoff climb out
Adjust for wind and maintain the runway centerline
Maneuver to the side of the runway or landing area when necessary to clear and avoid conflicting traffic
Ex: Go around was due to another airplane taking off. Unable to see them if directly overhead
Remain clear of obstacles/obstructions/other traffic
Wind Correction 										AI.VII.N.K4
Crab into the wind to maintain the extended centerline
Select two or more visual reference points directly ahead of the plane and keep them aligned
Occasionally glance back toward the runway to ensure the proper track and no drift
Use a moving map to align your track with the extended runway centerline
Communication
Once the airplane is under control, then communicate with the tower or other facility / aircraft
Let them know you’re “Going Around”
Aviate, Navigate, then Communicate
RM: Go-around with a LAHSO clearance (AIM 4-3-11 b(6)) 				AI.VII.N.R8
LAHSO clearance does not preclude a go-around
If necessary, execute the go-around, maintain safe separation from aircraft/vehicles, & notify ATC

Atmospheric Conditions

Wind
Headwinds increase climb performance (more airflow over the wings)
Tailwinds decrease climb performance (reduced airflow over the wings)
Common Errors 										AI.VII.N.K5
Failure to recognize a situation where a go-around/rejected landing is necessary
Hazards of delaying a decision to perform a go-around/rejected landing
Improper power application
Failure to control pitch attitude
Failure to compensate for torque effect
Improper trim procedure
Failure to maintain recommended airspeeds
Improper wing flaps or landing gear retraction procedure
Failure to maintain proper track during climb-out
Failure to remain well clear of obstructions and other traffic

They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation and ask them to stop

Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate

If SA or orientation is lost, admit it, and fix it

Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up

Collision Avoidance

Clearing Procedures
Descending: Execute gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Pattern: Scan for other traffic, enter traffic pattern at pattern altitude
Approach: Clear the runway
Uncontrolled Fields: Be conservative with spacing during takeoff, landing, and in the pattern

Day vs Night flying over terrain

Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’

Obstacles & Wire Strikes
Many structures can significantly affect safety below 500’ AGL and particularly below 200’ AGL
Obstacles can be found in the NOTAMs, and the Terminal Procedures (IFR document)
< 200’ AGL are unmarked/lighted power lines, antenna towers, etc.
Antenna Towers: Numerous antennas extend over 1,000’-2,000’ AGL
Most are supported by guy wires which can extend 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires: Wires and lines span runway departures and landmarks pilots frequently follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc. (may not be lit)
Airport Surface
Be alert for vehicles, persons, wildlife, or anything that could cause a hazard
Reject or delay takeoff, as required. Go around if landing
Scan vigilantly during taxi for aircraft and obstacles - If unsure of clearance, stop until you’re sure
Runway Incursion 										AI.VII.N.R9
Readback all hold short instructions
Review airport layouts
Review NOTAMs
Study & use proper phraseology
Maintain situational awareness – be aware of aircraft and their position in the pattern or on the field
A runway incursion from another aircraft may require a go-around
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points
